After a long discussion, Peter stood up and told them, “Brothers, you know that some time ago God chose me from among you to bring the message of the gospel to the Gentiles, so that they would hear it and believe.
And God, the knower of hearts, testified for them, granting them the Holy Spirit even as he granted him to us;
and he set no difference at all between them and us, when by faith he purified their hearts.
Now, then, why are you putting God to the test by laying on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have had strength to bear?
No — it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we believe we are saved, in the same way as they.”
The whole assembly fell silent, and they listened while Barnabas and Paul related what signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
After they finished speaking, James answered, “Brothers, hear me.
Simeon{b} has related how God first took thought to take from among the Gentiles a people for his name.
With this the words of the prophets agree, as it stands written,

‘After this I will return,
and I will rebuild the fallen tent of David;
its ruins I will rebuild,
and I will set it upright again,

that those remaining of mankind may search out the Lord,
and every nation upon whom my name is called,
says the Lord, who does these things,
known from of old.’{c}
My judgment, therefore, is that we should not make trouble for those among the Gentiles who are turning to God,
but should write to them to keep away from the pollutions of idols and from sexual immorality and from what is strangled and from blood.{d}
For Moses has had people preaching his Law in every city since ancient times, and it is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

Then the apostles and elders, with the agreement of the whole church, chose men from among their own number to send to Antioch along with Paul and Barnabas. They were Judas, called Barsabbas,{e} and Silas,{f} two men who held leading positions among the believers.

with this letter in their hand:{g}
“The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers of Gentile origin in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia: greetings.
Since we have heard that certain persons from among us, to whom we gave no instructions, have unsettled you with words, upsetting your minds,{h}
we have resolved, having come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you along with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have handed over their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who will tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no further burden than these necessary things:
keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. Guard yourselves against these and it will be well with you.{i} Be strong in health.”
So when they had been sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the assembly together, they delivered the letter.
And when they had read it, they rejoiced at the encouragement.
And Judas and Silas, who were themselves also prophets, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them.
And when they had passed some time there, the brothers released them with a blessing of peace to return to the ones who sent them.
But Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming, with many others also, the word of the Lord.
Some days later Paul told Barnabas, “We should return and check on the believers in every town where we announced the word of the Lord, to find out how they are doing.”
Barnabas wanted to take along with them John also, who was called Mark.
Paul, however, did not consider it fitting to bring along the man who had deserted them back in Pamphylia and had not stayed with them for the work.
And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they parted company; Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and departed, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.{k}
And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

notes.text: Codex Bezae adds “and walk according to the custom of Moses,” and in 15:2 says that Paul had told them to remain as they were when they believed.
Simeon: Peter’s Hebrew name, Shimon, “he has heard.”

Amos 9:11–12 (Greek), with Isa 45:21. The Hebrew of Amos 9:12 reads “that they may possess the remnant of Edom.” For “known from of old,” many later manuscripts read “Known to God from of old are all his works.”

The Western text (Codex Bezae and others) omits “what is strangled” here and in 15:29, and adds the negative Golden Rule: “and not to do to others what they would not want done to themselves.” This turns the decree from food laws into moral precepts (idolatry, immorality, bloodshed).
Barsabbas: probably “son of the sabbath”; the meaning is uncertain.
Silas: a Semitic name, perhaps from Aramaic *sheila*, “asked”; Paul calls him Silvanus (1 Thess 1:1). The meaning is uncertain.
With this letter in their hand: literally “having written by their hand.”
Many later manuscripts add “saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the Law.’”
You will do well: Codex Bezae adds “being borne along by the Holy Spirit.”

Verse 34: the Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts do not include verse 34; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Some manuscripts, including Codex Bezae and Ephraemi, add “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there,” and Bezae continues, “and Judas journeyed alone.” The addition explains why Silas is in Antioch in 15:40.
Of the Lord: many manuscripts read “of God.”

verses.text: He arrived too at Derbe, and at Lystra. A certain disciple was there by the name of Timothy,{a} whose mother was a believing Jewess, while his father was Greek.
The brothers in Lystra and Iconium gave a good report of him.
Paul wanted him to go with him; and he took him and circumcised him on account of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they traveled from town to town, they passed on to the believers the decisions made by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to follow.
So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew in numbers daily.
They went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia,{b} having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.{c}
When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus{d} did not allow them.
So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, pleading with him and saying, “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.”
As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we{e} tried to find passage to Macedonia, since we were sure that God had called us to give them the good news.
Setting sail, then, from Troas, we ran a straight course to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis,
and thence to Philippi, foremost city of that part of Macedonia,{f} a Roman colony. Some days we spent in this city.
And on the sabbath day we went outside the gate beside a river, where we supposed there was a place of prayer;{g} and sitting down, we spoke to the women who had come together.
Among our hearers was a God-fearing woman by the name of Lydia,{h} a seller of purple goods, from the city of Thyatira, whose heart the Lord opened to give heed to Paul’s words.
And when she had been baptized, and her household, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” And she prevailed on us.
Once, on our way to the place of prayer, we encountered a slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination,{i} who by her soothsaying brought her masters large profits.
She followed Paul and the rest of us, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, and they are telling you how to be saved.”
This she kept doing for many days. Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.
Her masters, seeing that the hope of their profits had departed, laid hold of Paul and Silas and hauled them to the marketplace in front of the authorities.
And having brought them to the magistrates,{j} they said, “These men are throwing our city into an uproar. They are Jews,
and they teach practices that we, being Romans, are not permitted to adopt or to observe.”
The mob also rose up together against them, and the magistrates ripped their clothes from them and ordered them flogged with rods.
After beating them severely, they threw them into prison and told the jailer to guard them carefully.
He, on receiving an order like this, cast them into the innermost cell and made their feet fast in the wooden stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them,
and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and [immediately] all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened.
When the jailer woke and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out with a loud voice, “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.”
Calling for lights, the jailer sprang inside and, quaking, threw himself down before Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
And they spoke the word of the Lord{k} to him and to all who were in his house.
And taking them at that hour of the night, he bathed the stripes from their backs; and immediately he was baptized, he and all who were his.
Then, leading them up into his home, he spread a table before them, and with all his house he was full of joy at having come to believe in God.
But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police{l} with the message, “Let those men go.”
And the jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent word to let you go. So come out now and go in peace.”

But Paul answered them, “Without a trial they flogged us in public, Roman citizens though we are, and cast us into prison — and are they now to put us out quietly? Not at all! Let them come in person and escort us out.”
The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens.
So they came and pleaded with them, and bringing them out, they begged them to depart from the city.{m}
After leaving the prison, they went to Lydia’s house. There they met with the believers and encouraged them, and then they left.

notes.text: Timothy: Greek, “honoring God.”
The region of Phrygia and Galatia: or “Phrygia and the Galatian region.”
Asia: the Roman province in western Asia Minor.
The Spirit of Jesus: this unusual expression is in the earliest manuscripts; later manuscripts read simply “the Spirit.”
We: here the first of the “we” passages in Acts begins (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), traditionally taken to mean the author joined Paul.

A leading city of the district of Macedonia: so the Westcott–Hort text (literally “first city of the part of Macedonia”); the Greek is difficult, and some editors adopt a conjectural reading, “a city of the first district of Macedonia.” Macedonia was divided into four districts.
Place of prayer: Greek *proseuchē*, often used of a synagogue.
Lydia: a name meaning “the Lydian woman”; Thyatira was in the region of Lydia.
A spirit of divination: literally “a spirit, a python,” after the serpent Python of the oracle at Delphi.
Magistrates: Greek *stratēgoi*, the chief officials of the colony.
Police: Greek *rhabdouchoi*, “rod-bearers,” the attendants of the magistrates (Latin *lictores*).
Of the Lord: some early manuscripts read “of God.”

Codex Bezae greatly expands 16:35–40: the magistrates come “to the market place” and, “remembering the earthquake,” are afraid; they beg Paul and Silas, “We did not know the truth about you, that you are righteous men,” and ask them to leave lest the crowd turn on them again.

verses.text: Taking the road through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they arrived at Thessalonica, where the Jews had a synagogue.
Paul, as his habit was, went in among them, and over three sabbaths he reasoned with them out of the Scriptures,
He explained and showed that the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am telling you about,” he said, “is the Messiah.”
Some of them were convinced and threw in their lot with Paul and Silas, as did a great crowd of God-fearing Greeks and not a few of the foremost women.

But the Jews grew jealous, and taking along some wicked fellows from the marketplace rabble, they gathered a mob and set the city in an uproar. They descended on Jason’s{a} house, seeking to bring Paul and Silas out to the people’s assembly.{b}
Not finding them there, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the city officials,{c} bawling out, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too,
and Jason has taken them in! They all act against the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, Jesus.”
At these words both the crowd and the politarchs became agitated;
and only after taking security from Jason and the others did they let them go.
Immediately, under cover of night, the brothers sent Paul and Silas away to Beroea, and on their arrival there they went off to the synagogue of the Jews.
These Jews were of nobler mind than those in Thessalonica: they took in the word with all eagerness, sifting the Scriptures day after day to see whether these things held true.
Many of them, therefore, became believers, along with no small number of Greek women of standing and of men.
But once the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul in Beroea too, there also they came, agitating and stirring up the crowds.
Then the brothers at once sent Paul off to make his way to the sea, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind there.
Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens; and with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him with all possible speed, they departed.
Now while Paul waited for them in Athens, his spirit was roused within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.
So he debated in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles, and daily in the public square with whoever was present.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also engaged him in debate. And some were saying, “What would this seed-picker{d} wish to say?” Others, “He seems to be a herald of foreign divinities” — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection.{e}
So they took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus,{f} saying, “May we learn what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
For you are bringing some strange notions to our ears; we want, then, to know what these things mean.”
(Now all the Athenians and the foreigners residing there had leisure for nothing else than telling or hearing something newer.)

Paul stood up in front of the Areopagus and said:
“People of Athens, I see that you are very religious in every way.{g}

For as I was passing through and looking over the objects of your worship, I found also an altar on which had been inscribed, ‘To an unknown god.’ What therefore you worship without knowing, this I announce to you.
The God who made the world and all that is in it — he, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in shrines made by hands,
nor is he waited on by human hands as if he lacked anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things.
And from one{h} he made every nation of humankind to dwell on all the face of the earth, having fixed appointed seasons and the boundaries of their habitation,
God did this so that they would search for him and perhaps reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from any one of us.

‘In him we live and move and exist.’ As some of your own poets have said,
‘We are also his children.’{i}
Being, then, God’s offspring, we ought not to think the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, a thing engraved by human art and imagination.
God, then, has looked past the times of not knowing; but at present he is announcing to humanity that everyone in every place must repent,
because he has set a day on which he is about to judge the inhabited world in righteousness by a man whom he has designated, having furnished proof to all by raising him from the dead.”
When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some of them mocked, but others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.”
So Paul went out from among them.
Some people did side with him and believe. They included Dionysius, who sat on the Areopagus court,{j} a woman called Damaris,{k} and several others.

notes.text: Jason: a Greek name, “healer,” often used by Jews named Joshua (Jesus).
People’s assembly: Greek *dēmos*, the citizen body of a free city; or simply “the crowd.”
City officials: Greek *politarchas*, “politarchs,” the title of the magistrates of Thessalonica, attested in inscriptions.
Seed-picker: Greek *spermologos*, a bird that picks up seeds; used of an idle babbler who picks up scraps of learning.
Jesus and the resurrection: some hearers may have taken “Resurrection” (*Anastasis*) as the name of a goddess paired with Jesus.
Areopagus: “hill of Ares,” the Greek god of war; also the name of the council that met there.
Exceedingly religious: or “very superstitious”; Greek *deisidaimonesterous*.
From one: many later manuscripts read “from one blood.”
The words “in him we live and move and have our being” are thought to echo the Cretan poet Epimenides; the quoted line is from Aratus, *Phaenomena* 5.
Areopagite: a member of the council of the Areopagus.
Damaris: the meaning is uncertain; perhaps a form of *damalis*, “heifer.” Codex Bezae omits her name.

verses.text: After this Paul left Athens and came to Corinth.
There he came upon a Jew named Aquila,{a} a native of Pontus, lately arrived from Italy with Priscilla{b} his wife because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome.{c} He went to see them,
and since their craft was his own he lodged with them and they plied it together; tentmaking{d} was their trade.
And every sabbath he would argue in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to preaching, and he declared to the Jews that Jesus was the Messiah.
And when they set themselves against him and spoke abusively, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
Moving on from there, he entered the home of one Titius Justus,{e} a God-fearer, whose house stood next door to the synagogue.
Crispus,{f} the synagogue ruler, came to believe in the Lord, along with all his household; and many of the Corinthians who heard believed and were baptized.
Then the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Have no fear; keep on speaking, and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one shall lay a hand on you to harm you, because I have many people in this city.”
So he settled there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia,{g} the Jews rose up in concert against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
and charging, “This man is inducing people to revere God against the law.”
Paul was about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were some misdeed or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to bear with you;
but if these are questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. A judge of such matters I refuse to be.”
So he had them driven from the tribunal.
Then everyone{h} grabbed Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the judge’s seat. But Gallio showed no concern about any of this.
Paul remained many days more, then bade the brothers farewell and set sail for Syria, Priscilla and Aquila with him, having shorn his head at Cenchreae, since he had taken a vow.{i}
They came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
They pressed him to remain longer, but he would not consent;
but on taking leave of them he said, “I will come back to you again, if God wills,”{j} and he set sail from Ephesus.
When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up{k} and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
Having spent a while there, he set out and passed in turn through the Galatian country and Phrygia, giving strength to all the disciples.
Meanwhile there arrived at Ephesus a certain Jew, Apollos{l} by name, Alexandrian by birth, a learned man and mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had received instruction in the way of the Lord. He was passionate in spirit, and he taught accurately about Jesus, though the only baptism he knew was John’s.
He began to speak out boldly in the synagogue; but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the Way of God{m} more accurately.
He wanted to go across into Achaia, so the brothers urged him on and wrote asking the disciples to receive him. After he came, he was of great service to the ones who by grace had come to believe;{n}
for with force he confuted the Jews openly, demonstrating from the Scriptures that the Messiah was Jesus.

notes.text: Aquila: Latin, “eagle.”
Priscilla: a diminutive of the Latin Prisca, “ancient, venerable.”
The emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49 (Suetonius, *Claudius* 25.4).
Tentmakers: Greek *skēnopoioi*; possibly “leatherworkers.”
Titius Justus: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus; Sinaiticus reads “Titus Justus,” and many manuscripts simply “Justus.”
Crispus: Latin, “curly.”
Gallio … proconsul of Achaia: Lucius Junius Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca; an inscription at Delphi places his proconsulship in AD 51–52.
They all: many later manuscripts read “all the Greeks.”
He was under a vow: probably a Nazirite vow or one like it (Num 6:1–21); grammatically, the one who cut his hair might be Aquila.
If God wills: many later manuscripts, following Codex Bezae, add before this, “I must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem.”
He went up: that is, to Jerusalem.
Apollos: short for Apollonius, from the god Apollo.
The Way of God: some manuscripts read “the Way of the Lord,” and others “the Way.”
Codex Bezae rewrites 18:27, saying that some Corinthians staying in Ephesus urged Apollos to come to their country.

verses.text: It came about, while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having passed through the inland regions,{a} came down to Ephesus, where he found certain disciples.
“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you came to believe?” he asked them. They replied, “No — we have not so much as heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.”
“Into what, then, were you baptized?” he said. “Into John’s baptism,” said they.
Paul answered, “John’s was a baptism of repentance; he told the people that their faith must rest on him who was to come after — on Jesus, that is.”
On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying.
There were about twelve men in all.
He went into the synagogue and for three months spoke out boldly, debating and persuading about the kingdom of God.

But when some grew hardened and would not believe, maligning the Way before the gathering, he withdrew from them, took the disciples apart with him, and day by day held discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.{b}
This went on for two years, so that every inhabitant of Asia, Jew and Greek, heard the word of the Lord.
And God was working miracles of no ordinary kind by Paul’s hands,
so much so that cloths and aprons{c} were taken from his body to those who were ill, and they were rid of their sicknesses and the wicked spirits departed.
Some traveling Jewish exorcists tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus over people who had evil spirits. They said, “I command you in the name of the Jesus that Paul preaches.”
Seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish high priest,{d} were doing this.
But the evil spirit retorted to them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I am acquainted with; but you — who are you?”
Then the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered them both,{e} and so prevailed against them that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the residents of Ephesus, Jews and Greeks alike; fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.
Many of those who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their practices.{f}

And a good number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. When they reckoned up the value of them, it came to fifty thousand days’ wages.{g}
So mightily did the word of the Lord grow and prevail.
When all this was accomplished, Paul purposed in the Spirit{h} to travel by way of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must see Rome as well.”
He sent two of his assistants, Timothy and Erastus,{i} to Macedonia, while he himself remained in Asia a little longer.
About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.
For a silversmith named Demetrius, who made [silver] shrines of Artemis,{j} was bringing the craftsmen no small business.
He gathered them together, along with the workers in similar trades, and said, “Gentlemen, you know that we make a good living from this business.

You are looking on and hearing how, not at Ephesus only but over nearly the whole of Asia, this Paul has won over a sizable crowd and led them astray, by telling them that handmade gods are no gods at all.

It is not merely this line of ours that risks falling into contempt; the sanctuary of the mighty goddess Artemis also stands to be reckoned as nothing, and she is about to be stripped of her majesty, she whom the whole of Asia and the world revere.”
When they heard this, they were filled with rage and kept shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
So the whole city was filled with turmoil, and with one impulse they surged into the theater, seizing as they went Gaius and Aristarchus,{k} Macedonians traveling with Paul.
Paul wanted to go in among the people, but the disciples would not let him;
and even some of the officials of the province,{l} who were friends of his, sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theater.
Now some were crying one thing, some another; the assembly was a confused mass, and the greater part had no idea for what purpose they had assembled.
Some in the crowd instructed Alexander, since the Jews had thrust him to the front; and Alexander, waving his hand for silence, was ready to offer a defense before the populace.
But when they recognized that he was a Jew, a single cry went up from them all, and for about two hours they kept shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The town clerk{m} finally calmed the mob and said, “Ephesians, what man alive is unaware that Ephesus is guardian of the temple{n} of great Artemis and of the image fallen from heaven?{o}
Since, then, these things cannot be contradicted, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
So if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a case against somebody, court days are held and proconsuls sit; let the parties bring their accusations there.
And should you want anything beyond that, the matter will be resolved in the regular assembly.
For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, there being no cause that we can give to account for this commotion.”
And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

notes.text: The inland regions: literally “the upper parts,” the highlands of Asia Minor. Codex Bezae begins the verse: “But when Paul wished, according to his own plan, to go to Jerusalem, the Spirit told him to return to Asia.”

Tyrannus: Greek, “tyrant, ruler,” probably the owner of the hall or a teacher who lectured there. Codex Bezae adds “from eleven in the morning until four in the afternoon” (literally “from the fifth hour to the tenth”), the hours of the midday rest.
Handkerchiefs or aprons: Latin loanwords in Greek, *soudaria* and *simikinthia*; probably sweat cloths and work aprons.
A Jewish high priest: no Sceva is known among the high priests; he may have been of a high-priestly family or claimed the title.
Both: or “all of them”; the Greek *amphoterōn* sometimes means “all” in later Greek.
Practices: Greek *praxeis*, perhaps in the technical sense of magic spells.
Fifty thousand days’ wages: literally “fifty thousand of silver,” that is, silver coins, probably drachmas, each roughly a day’s wage for a laborer.
In the Spirit: or “in his spirit.”
Erastus: Greek, “beloved.”

Artemis: the Greek goddess identified with the Roman Diana; the Artemis of Ephesus was a mother goddess whose temple was one of the seven wonders of the world. The shrines were probably small models of the temple.
Gaius and Aristarchus: Gaius is a common Latin name; Aristarchus, Greek, “best ruler.”
Officials of the province: Greek *Asiarchōn*, “Asiarchs,” leading men of the province of Asia.
Town clerk: Greek *grammateus*, the chief civic official of Ephesus.
Temple keeper: Greek *neōkoros*, an honorary title of cities that maintained the temple of a deity or of the emperor.
The sacred stone that fell from the sky: literally “the fallen-from-Zeus [thing],” probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verses.text: When the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples and, after encouraging them, said farewell and set out for Macedonia.
When he had gone through those parts and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece.
where he stayed for three months. Because the Jews plotted against him just as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia.{a}
He was accompanied by Sopater the son of Pyrrhus, of Beroea; of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; Gaius of Derbe,{b} and Timothy; and from Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.{c}
These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas;
As for us, we set sail out of Philippi once the days of Unleavened Bread were over, and five days later joined them in Troas, where we remained a week.
On the first day of the week we met to break bread. Paul spoke to the people, and since he was going to leave the next day, he kept on talking until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.
And a young man named Eutychus,{d} sitting at the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. Overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story{e} and was picked up dead.
Paul, however, went down, flung himself upon him, and clasping him said, “Stop your lamenting; his life is still in him.”
Then he climbed back up, broke the bread, and ate; and after speaking with them at length, till dawn, he left.
And they brought the lad home living, and were greatly comforted.
We, meanwhile, went before him to the ship and put out for Assos, where we were to pick Paul up; this was his arrangement, as he meant to make the journey on foot.
When he joined us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos;{f} and the day after that we came to Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail on past Ephesus and not lose time in Asia; he was pressing on, if at all possible, to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost day.
Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him.

On their arrival he addressed them:
“You know well what my conduct was with you all along, from the day I first stepped into Asia:
slaving for the Lord in all lowliness of mind, in tears, and in the testings that came upon me from the Jews’ plotting;
how I held back nothing that would benefit you, but declared it to you and taught you openly and in your homes,
bearing solemn witness to Jews and Greeks alike of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.{g}
And now, see, bound by the Spirit{h} I am on my way to Jerusalem, unaware of what I shall meet with there,
save that city after city the Holy Spirit warns me solemnly that chains and hardships lie in wait for me.
Yet I hold my life worth nothing, not precious to me at all, so long as I complete my race and the service the Lord Jesus entrusted to me, of bearing witness to the good news of God’s grace.{i}
And now, see, this I know: you will none of you look upon my face again — you all, among whom I went about heralding the kingdom.
For that reason I solemnly declare to you on this very day: I am clean of everyone’s blood,
for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.
Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock that the Holy Spirit has put in your care as overseers.{j} Be shepherds of the church of God,{k} which he bought with his own blood.{l}
I know that once I have gone, savage wolves will make their way in among you and will not spare the flock;
yes, out of your own number men will rise up uttering perversions, so as to lure the disciples away after themselves.
Keep awake, then, and remember that for a three-year stretch, by night and by day, I never stopped warning each of you, with tears.
And now I commend you to the Lord{m} and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel.
You know very well that I worked with my own hands to meet my needs and the needs of my companions.

In everything I have given you an example: that toiling thus we ought to come to the aid of the weak, keeping in mind the saying of the Lord Jesus himself, ‘More blessed is giving than receiving.’”{n}
And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all.
They all wept freely, and falling on Paul’s neck they kissed him again and again,
grieved above all at the word he had said, that they were never more to see his face. Then they went with him down to the ship.

notes.text: Codex Bezae reads, “he wished to sail to Syria, but the Spirit told him to return through Macedonia.”
Gaius of Derbe: Codex Bezae reads “Gaius of Doberus,” a town in Macedonia, which would make him the Macedonian Gaius of 19:29.
Tychicus and Trophimus: Greek names, “fortunate” and “nourishing, foster child.” Many manuscripts add after “accompanied by” the words “as far as Asia.”
Eutychus: Greek, “fortunate.”
Third story: Greek *tristegou*.
Many later manuscripts add “at Trogyllium, and stayed there,” after “Samos.”
Our Lord Jesus: many manuscripts read “our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Constrained by the Spirit: or “bound in spirit.”

The text of this verse varies considerably among the manuscripts. Many later ones have a longer form in which Paul says that none of these things disturbs him and that he places no value on his own life, so long as he can complete his mission with joy.
Overseers: Greek *episkopous*, the word from which “bishop” derives.

The church of God: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Many manuscripts, including Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Codex Bezae, and the papyrus P74 (as reported), read “the church of the Lord,” and many later manuscripts conflate the two: “the church of the Lord and God.” The harder reading “of God” is generally preferred.

With the blood of his own: or “with his own blood.” Westcott and Hort suggested the meaning is “with the blood of his own [Son],” taking *tou idiou* as a title; many later manuscripts read “with his own blood” in a different word order.
The Lord: many manuscripts read “God.”
This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels.

verses.text: When we had torn ourselves away from them and put to sea, we ran a straight course to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and thence to Patara.{a}
Finding there a ship bound across to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.
We sighted Cyprus, passed it on our left, and sailed on to Syria. We landed at Tyre, where the ship was to unload its cargo.
We sought out the disciples and stopped there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to set foot in Jerusalem.
But when our days there were ended, we left and went on our way, and all of them, with wives and children, escorted us till we were outside the city. Kneeling on the beach, we prayed
and bade one another goodbye; then we boarded the ship, and they went back home.
Completing the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and spent a day with them.
Departing on the morrow, we came to Caesarea and entered the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven, and lodged with him.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
While we were staying on there for a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came over to us, took up Paul’s girdle, tied his own feet and hands, and declared, “The Holy Spirit says this: ‘The owner of this girdle the Jews in Jerusalem will tie up just so, and hand over into Gentile hands.’”
On hearing this, both we and the people of the place pleaded with him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul replied, “What are you about, weeping and crushing my heart? For my part, I stand ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
And since he would not be persuaded, we held our peace, saying only, “The Lord’s will be done.”
After those days we packed{b} and started up to Jerusalem.
Certain disciples from Caesarea traveled with us too, conducting us to one Mnason, a Cypriot and an early disciple, at whose home we were to be guests.{c}
On our reaching Jerusalem the brothers made us gladly welcome.
On the following day Paul went with us to James’s, and the elders all came.
After greeting them, he gave a detailed account, one thing after another, of what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
They glorified God when they heard it, and said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have believed — and every one of them a zealot for the Law.
They have heard it said of you that you instruct all the Jews living among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, and that you tell them to stop circumcising their children and living by our customs.
What, then? No doubt they will learn of your arrival.{d}
So do what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow.

Join these men, undergo purification with them, and bear the cost for them to have their heads shaved. So everybody will recognize that the reports about you amount to nothing, and that you too keep in line, observing the Law.
As regards the Gentile believers, we have written them our decision, that they guard themselves from what is offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication.”{e}

Then Paul took the men, and the next day, having purified himself with them, he went into the temple, giving notice of when the days of purification would be completed and the offering presented for each one of them.
As the seven days were about to end, some Jews from the province of Asia noticed Paul in the temple. They agitated the entire crowd and seized him,

crying out, “Israelites, help! This is the man who goes everywhere teaching everyone to oppose our people, our Law, and this place. On top of that, he has brought Greeks into the temple and desecrated this holy place.”
(They had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city earlier, and they assumed that Paul had taken him into the temple.)
The whole city was set in motion, and the people came running together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and immediately the gates were shut.
As they were trying to kill him, word went up to the tribune{f} of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
At once he took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them; and when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came over, arrested him, and ordered that he be tied up with two chains. Then he asked who Paul was and what he had done.
In the crowd, though, some yelled this and some that; and as the din kept him from learning anything certain, he gave orders for Paul to be taken to the barracks.
When Paul came to the steps, he had actually to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the mob,
for the mass of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!”
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the commander, “May I speak with you?” The commander asked, “Do you speak Greek?
Are you not, then, that Egyptian who lately raised an insurrection and took the four thousand Assassins{g} out to the wilderness?”
“I am a Jewish man,” said Paul, “of Tarsus in Cilicia, citizen of a city of some note. I ask you, allow me to address the people.”
The commander gave permission, so Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the people. When it became quiet, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language,{h} saying:

notes.text: Patara: Codex Bezae and some others add “and Myra.”
We packed: or “we made ready,” possibly “we saddled horses.”
Codex Bezae reads, “These brought us to the village where we were to lodge with Mnason,” placing Mnason’s home on the way to Jerusalem.
Many manuscripts add, “A multitude must certainly come together, for they will hear that you have come.”
Codex Bezae and others add “that they should observe no such thing except to keep themselves from,” and omit “what is strangled” (compare 15:20).
Tribune: Greek *chiliarchos*, “commander of a thousand,” the officer in command of the Roman cohort in the Antonia fortress.

Assassins: Greek *sikariōn*, from Latin *sicarii*, “dagger men,” Jewish insurgents who stabbed their opponents in crowds. Josephus tells of an Egyptian false prophet who led a large following to the Mount of Olives about AD 54.
The Hebrew language: probably Aramaic, the common language of the Jews of Palestine.

verses.text: “Brothers and fathers, hear the defense I am making to you now.”
And on hearing him speak to them in the Hebrew tongue, they kept still all the more. Then he said:
“A Jew am I, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, yet brought up here in this city at Gamaliel’s feet, trained exactly in the Law of our fathers, and as full of zeal for God as all of you are this day.
This Way I hounded to the death, putting men and women alike in fetters and handing them over to prisons —

to which the high priest bears me out, and all the body of elders. Letters from them I carried to the brothers in Damascus, and I traveled there to fetch those who were there back to Jerusalem in bonds, for their punishment.
“Now it came about, as I journeyed and neared Damascus around midday, that suddenly out of the sky a powerful light blazed all about me.
I dropped to the ground and heard a voice say to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you hunting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, the one you are hunting.’
My companions beheld the light,{a} yet they did not catch the voice of him who was talking with me.
Then I said, ‘Lord, what am I to do?’ The Lord told me, ‘Rise and continue into Damascus; there you shall be told everything it is laid down for you to do.’
And as I was sightless because of the glory of that light, my companions took me by the hand and so I came into Damascus.
“Then a certain Ananias, a man reverent according to the Law and well attested by all the Jews dwelling there,
he came to me, took his stand by my side, and told me, ‘Saul, my brother, see again!’ And in the same hour I could see, and I looked upon him.{b}
And he said, ‘The God of our fathers has chosen you beforehand to know his will, to see the Just One, and to hear speech from his own mouth;
because to all mankind you are to be his witness of the things you have seen and heard.
And now, why delay? Get up and be baptized and have your sins washed away, calling upon his name.’
“It happened, after my return to Jerusalem, that as I prayed in the temple I came to be in a trance,
and I saw him, and he said to me, ‘Hurry, leave Jerusalem without delay; for they will not receive what you testify concerning me.’
And I said, ‘Lord, they know well enough that from synagogue to synagogue I used to jail and whip the people who believed on you;
and when the blood of your witness{c} Stephen was poured out, I too was there, standing near, consenting to it, and minding the clothes of his killers.’
Then he told me, ‘Go; it is to the nations far off that I shall send you.’”
They had given him a hearing until this word; but now they lifted up their voices: “Rid the earth of such a man! It is not fit that he should live!”
And while they bellowed and tossed their garments about and hurled dust in the air,
the tribune commanded that he be taken into the barracks, directing that he be questioned under the lash, so he might discover the cause of their outcry against him.
As they tied him forward with the straps,{d} Paul said to the centurion standing there, “Are you allowed to scourge a man who is a Roman, and that without a verdict?”
Hearing this, the centurion went off to the tribune with the report: “What are you going to do? This man is a Roman.”
The tribune came up and asked him, “Say: are you a Roman?” “I am,” said he.
And the tribune replied, “I paid a heavy price for this citizenship of mine.”{e} “I, though,” said Paul, “have been a citizen from birth.”
At that, the men who were to interrogate him stepped back from him at once; and the tribune too grew fearful, once he knew Paul was a Roman and he had put him in chains.

The following day, wishing to know for certain what accusation the Jews were bringing, he loosed him and ordered the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin to assemble; and bringing Paul down, he stood him before them.

notes.text: Beheld the light: many later manuscripts add “and were afraid.” Compare 9:7.
I could see, and I looked upon him: or “I looked up at him”; the Greek *anablepsa* has both senses.
Witness: Greek *martys*, the word that later came to mean “martyr.”
Tied him forward with the straps: or “stretched him out for the lashes.”

A heavy price: literally “a great sum of money.” Citizenship could be obtained through bribery of officials under Claudius; the tribune’s name, Claudius Lysias (23:26), suggests he took the emperor’s name on becoming a citizen.

verses.text: Fixing his gaze on the Sanhedrin, Paul said, “Brothers, with a wholly good conscience I have conducted myself as God’s citizen until this very day.”
At that, Ananias{a} the high priest directed the men standing near him to hit him across the mouth.
Paul then said to him, “God will strike you, you limewashed wall! You sit judging me by the Law, and against the Law you bid them strike me?”
The bystanders said, “Is it God’s high priest you are insulting?”
Paul answered, “Brothers, I was unaware that he was high priest; for Scripture says, ‘A ruler of your people you shall not curse.’”{b}

But Paul, aware that some of them were Sadducees and others Pharisees, called out in the Sanhedrin, “Brothers, a Pharisee am I, born of Pharisees! I am being judged over our hope, the rising of the dead.”
No sooner had he said it than strife broke out between Pharisees and Sadducees, and the gathering was split in two.
(Sadducees hold that there is neither resurrection nor angel nor spirit, while Pharisees confess both.)
A loud outcry followed; and some scribes of the Pharisee side got up and fought it out: “Nothing evil do we find in the man. And suppose a spirit has spoken to him, or an angel?”{c}
As the strife grew great, the tribune feared they would tear Paul apart, and he ordered the troops to come down, snatch him out of their midst, and carry him to the barracks.
That next night the Lord came and stood beside him and said, “Be of good heart; just as you bore witness to me in Jerusalem, so in Rome too you must bear witness.”
At daybreak the Jews formed a conspiracy and put themselves under a curse,{d} vowing they would neither eat nor drink till Paul was dead.
Those who joined in this compact numbered over forty.
These approached the chief priests and the elders: “Under a solemn curse we have put ourselves to taste nothing until Paul is dead.

Now then, you and the Sanhedrin must signify to the tribune that he should bring him down before you, on the pretext of examining his affairs more thoroughly; and before ever he gets near, we stand prepared to do away with him.”
But Paul’s nephew, his sister’s son, got wind of the ambush; he came, went into the barracks, and reported it to Paul.
Paul summoned one of the centurions and said, “Bring this youth to the tribune; he has a report to make to him.”
So he took charge of him, led him before the tribune, and said, “The prisoner Paul called me over and requested me to bring this youth to you; he has something to tell you.”
The tribune took his hand, drew him aside, and asked him in private, “What is it you have to report to me?”
He said, “The Jews have arranged to ask you to bring Paul down to the Sanhedrin tomorrow, as if intending to look into his case with more care.

Do not give in to them, then; for upward of forty of them lie in wait for him, men who have cursed themselves not to eat or drink until they have done away with him; even now they stand ready, only awaiting your promise.”
So the tribune sent the youth away with a warning: “Breathe to nobody that you have made this known to me.”
Then, calling over a pair of his centurions, he said, “By nine o’clock tonight{e} have two hundred soldiers in readiness to march to Caesarea, along with seventy cavalry and two hundred spearmen;{f}
and have beasts on hand to mount Paul and convey him safe to Felix{g} the governor.”
And he wrote a letter in these terms:{h}
“Claudius Lysias to the most excellent Governor Felix: greeting.
The Jews had laid hold of this man and were on the point of killing him, when I intervened with my troops and took him from them, having found out that he is a Roman.
Wishing to ascertain the ground of their charges against him, [I brought him down to their Sanhedrin.]
I discovered that the charges concerned disputes over their Law, and that there was nothing against him worthy of death or of bonds.
Information then reached me of a plot to be carried out against the man, and I have forthwith dispatched him to you, directing his accusers as well to lay their case against him before you.”{i}
So the soldiers, as ordered, took charge of Paul and conducted him by night as far as Antipatris.{j}
On the morrow they went back to the barracks, leaving the cavalry to continue with him.
These, on entering Caesarea, handed the letter to the governor and presented Paul as well before him.
He read it and asked from which province Paul came; and learning it was Cilicia,
he said, “I will hear your case in full whenever your accusers also are here,” and he ordered him kept under guard in Herod’s praetorium.{k}

notes.text: Ananias: high priest about AD 47–59; the name is Hebrew Hananiah, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Exod 22:28.
Many later manuscripts add, “Let us not fight against God.”
Put themselves under a curse: Greek *anathematizō*.
Nine o’clock tonight: literally “from the third hour of the night.”
Spearmen: the meaning of the rare Greek *dexiolabous* is uncertain; perhaps “bowmen,” “slingers,” or “led horses.”
Felix: Antonius Felix, procurator of Judea about AD 52–59; the name is Latin, “fortunate, happy.”

In these terms: or “of this kind.” Codex Bezae and some Latin manuscripts add, “for he was afraid that the Jews might seize Paul and kill him, and that he would afterward be accused of having taken a bribe.”
Many later manuscripts add “Farewell.”
Antipatris: a town about 37 miles (60 km) northwest of Jerusalem and 25 miles (40 km) south of Caesarea.
Praetorium: the governor’s residence, built as a palace by Herod the Great.

verses.text: Five days afterward the high priest Ananias came down, bringing certain elders and a pleader, one Tertullus,{a} and these laid their information against Paul before the governor.
When [he] had been called in, Tertullus opened the accusation thus: “Through you we enjoy great peace, and by your forethought reforms are coming about for this nation;
at every turn and in every place, most excellent Felix, we welcome it with the fullest gratitude.
But that I may not detain you longer, I entreat you of your forbearance to give us a brief hearing.
For we have found this fellow a very plague, a stirrer-up of riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.{b}
He even attempted to profane the temple; and so we took hold of him.{c}
From him, should you question him in person, you may ascertain the truth of everything of which we charge him.”
The Jews too joined in the attack, asserting that so these things stood.
The governor then gestured for Paul to speak, and Paul answered: “I know you have judged this nation for a good many years, and so I am glad to defend myself before you.
You are able to verify that not more than twelve days are past since I went up to worship at Jerusalem;
and neither in the temple did they find me arguing with anyone or gathering a crowd, nor in the synagogues, nor about the city.
Nor can they make good to you the charges they now bring against me.
This much I do confess to you: after the Way, which they call a sect, so do I serve the God of my fathers, believing all that accords with the Law and all that is written in the Prophets,
holding a hope toward God, which these men themselves also look for, that there is to be a resurrection of both righteous and unrighteous.
Therefore I too exercise myself to keep at all times a conscience void of offense toward God and toward men.
Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings;
in the midst of which they found me purified in the temple, with no crowd and no tumult. But some Jews from Asia —
these ought to be present before you to accuse me, if they had anything against me.
Or else let these men here say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the Sanhedrin,
unless it be this one cry which I uttered standing among them: ‘Over the resurrection of the dead I am under judgment before you this day.’”
Felix, though, being rather well informed concerning the Way, adjourned the hearing: “Once Lysias the tribune is down here,” said he, “I shall determine your matter.”
He directed the centurion to hold him under guard, yet with a measure of freedom, forbidding none of his friends to wait on him.
Some days later Felix arrived with Drusilla{e} his wife, who was a Jewess, and he sent for Paul and listened to him on faith in Christ Jesus.
But as he discoursed of righteousness and self-mastery and the judgment to come, Felix took fright and answered, “Go your way for the present; when I find a convenient season I will send for you.”
At the same time he was hoping too that money would be given [him] by Paul; on which account he sent for him all the oftener and conversed with him.
But when two years had run their course, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus;{f} and wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in bonds.

notes.text: Tertullus: a Latin name, a diminutive of Tertius, “third.” He was a professional advocate (Greek *rhētōr*, “orator”).
Nazarenes: the earliest Jewish name for the followers of Jesus, after Nazareth.
Took hold of him: the Westcott–Hort text ends the sentence here and continues directly with verse 8, so that “him” in verse 8 refers to Paul.

The Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts do not include verse 7 (with the end of verse 6 and the beginning of verse 8); the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Some later manuscripts, and the printed editions from Erasmus, include additional words saying that the speakers would have judged him by their own Law, but that Lysias the tribune intervened, took him from their hands by force, and ordered his accusers to appear before the governor. In that reading, “him” in verse 8 refers to Lysias.

Drusilla: a Latin name, a diminutive of Drusus (meaning uncertain). She was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I (12:1), who had left her first husband to marry Felix. Some Western witnesses add that it was she who wished to see Paul.
Festus: Porcius Festus, procurator of Judea about AD 59–62; the name is Latin, “festive, joyful.” Felix was recalled about AD 59.

verses.text: Festus, then, three days after setting foot in his province, went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid information before him against Paul, and they kept urging him,
begging as a favor to themselves, to his hurt, that he would summon him to Jerusalem — laying an ambush to make away with him on the road.
Festus answered, however, that Paul was being held at Caesarea, and that he himself would shortly be setting out thither.
“So let those among you who are men of standing,” said he, “go down with me, and if there is anything amiss in the man, let them accuse him.”
After staying among them no more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea; and on the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and commanded Paul to be brought.
When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood round him, bringing many and grave charges which they could not prove,
while Paul pleaded in his defense, “Neither against the Law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.”
But Festus, wishing to put the Jews under obligation, answered Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and there be judged on these matters before me?”
Said Paul, “At Caesar’s tribunal I stand, where I ought to be judged. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you too know very well.

If I am guilty and have done anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth in the charges these men bring against me, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
Then Festus, after conferring with his council, replied, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.”
When some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice{a} arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
As they were staying there a good many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left a prisoner by Felix,
about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews brought information, asking for sentence against him.
I told them that Romans have no custom of handing over anyone as a favor, before the accused has faced the accusers in person and had a chance to answer the charges.
When therefore they had assembled here, I lost no time; the day following I sat down upon the judgment seat and gave orders for the man to be fetched.
When the accusers stood up around him, they brought no charge of such evil deeds as I was supposing;
rather they had certain questions against him about their own religion{b} and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
Being at a loss how to inquire into these things, I asked whether he would go to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of His Majesty the Emperor,{c} I ordered him held until I could send him on to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear this man myself.” Festus replied, “Tomorrow you will hear him.”

Accordingly, on the morrow, there came Agrippa and Bernice amid much display, and they went into the hall of hearing with the tribunes and the city’s leading men; and Festus gave the word, and Paul was led in.

And Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all you men here present with us, you behold this man concerning whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, crying out that he ought not to live any longer.
But I found that he had done nothing deserving of death; and as he himself appealed to His Majesty, I determined to send him.

Yet I have nothing definite to write to my lord{d} about him. Therefore I have brought him out before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination has been held I may have something to write.
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to signify as well the charges against him.”

notes.text: Agrippa and Bernice: Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I (12:1), king of territories north and east of Galilee; the name is Latin, of uncertain meaning. Bernice, his sister, is the Macedonian form of Greek Pherenike, “bringer of victory.”
Religion: or “superstition” (Greek *deisidaimonia*); compare 17:22.
His Majesty the Emperor: Greek *ho Sebastos*, “the Revered One,” the Greek equivalent of the title Augustus; here Nero.
My lord: Greek *kyrios*, used of the emperor.

verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “Leave is given you to speak on your own behalf.” Then Paul stretched forth his hand and made his defense:
“Touching all the things whereof I am accused by Jews, King Agrippa, I count myself fortunate that it is before you I am to answer for myself today,
the more so because you are expert in all the customs and controversies among Jews. I pray you, therefore, hear me out with patience.
“My manner of life from youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem, all Jews know,
having known me a long while, if only they would bear witness, that after the strictest party of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
And now for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers I stand here on trial,
a promise our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. For this hope, O king, I am accused by Jews!
Why is it judged a thing past belief among you, if God raises the dead?
“I myself, indeed, once thought it my duty to do many things in opposition to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And this I did in Jerusalem: many of the saints I shut up in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were put to death I cast my vote{a} against them.
In all the synagogues I often had them punished and tried to make them blaspheme. I was so furiously angry at them that I even chased them to cities in foreign lands.
“On such an errand I was journeying to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests,
when at midday, O king, I saw on the road a light out of heaven, brighter than the brilliance of the sun, shining round about me and those who journeyed with me.
And when we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language,{b} ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’{c}
I asked, ‘Lord, who are you?’ The Lord replied, ‘Jesus am I, whom you persecute.

But rise and stand upon your feet; for to this end have I appeared to you, to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things in which you have seen me{d} and of those in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you,

I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they will turn from the dark to the light, and from Satan’s control to God. Then they will receive forgiveness of sins and a share with those who have been made holy by trusting in me.’
Hence, King Agrippa, to that vision from heaven I was not disobedient,
but to them of Damascus first, and at Jerusalem, and over all the region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I proclaimed that they must repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of repentance.
On this account Jews seized me in the temple and tried to make an end of me.
Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day bearing witness to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said should come to pass:
that the Messiah was to suffer, and that he, first of the resurrection from the dead, would proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”
And as he was so making his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “You are mad, Paul! Your great learning is turning you to madness.”
But Paul said, “I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but am uttering words of truth and soberness.
For the king knows of these matters, and to him I speak with boldness; for I am persuaded that none of these things escapes his notice, since this was not done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a little you would persuade me to play the Christian!”{e}
And Paul said, “I would pray to God that, whether in little or in much, not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — save for these chains.”
Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice, and those who sat with them;
and when they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing deserving death or imprisonment.”
And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set at liberty, had he not appealed to Caesar.”

notes.text: Cast my vote: literally “brought down a pebble,” the voting stone; whether Paul had a formal vote in the Sanhedrin is uncertain, and the phrase may simply mean “I gave my approval.”
The Hebrew language: probably Aramaic.
Kick against the goads: a Greek proverb for useless resistance, from an ox kicking against the pointed stick of its driver.
Seen me: some manuscripts read “have seen.”

In a little you would persuade me to play the Christian: the Greek is difficult. It may mean “In a short time,” or “With so little,” and the verb may mean “persuade me to become” or “persuade me to act as.” Many later manuscripts read “You almost persuade me to become a Christian.”

verses.text: Now when it was resolved that we should sail away for Italy, they handed over Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius,{a} of the Augustan Cohort.{b}
Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium,{c} which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, there being with us Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica.
The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius treated Paul with kindness and allowed him to visit his friends so they could provide for his needs.
Putting out from thence, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us.
And when we had sailed across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.{d}
There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and put us aboard her.
Many a day we crept along slowly and with much ado got abreast of Cnidus; then, the wind forbidding our approach, we slipped under the lee of Crete by Salmone.
Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was the town of Lasea.
Much time having now been spent, and the voyage being already perilous because even the Fast{e} was already gone by, Paul gave them warning,
saying to them, “Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with injury and heavy loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”
But the centurion paid more heed to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to the things spoken by Paul.

And because the harbor was ill suited to winter in, the majority advised putting out from there, in hope that they might somehow reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete looking toward the southwest and northwest,{f} and winter there.
When a south wind blew softly, supposing they had gained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, hugging the shore.
But not long after, there rushed down from it a tempestuous wind, the one called Euraquilo.{g}
And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.
Darting in to the shelter of a small island named Cauda,{h} we barely managed to secure the skiff.
After hoisting it up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and fearing lest they should run aground on the Syrtis,{i} they lowered the gear,{j} and so were driven along.
As we were exceedingly storm-tossed, the next day they began to throw cargo overboard;
and the third day they flung out the ship’s furniture with their own hands.
And when neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay upon us, all hope of our being saved was at last being taken away.
When they had long gone without food, Paul stood up in their midst and said, “Sirs, you ought to have hearkened to me and not have set sail from Crete, and so have been spared this injury and loss.
Yet now I counsel you to take heart; for there shall be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For there stood by me this night an angel of the God whose I am and whom I serve,
and he told me, ‘Paul, have no fear. You are going to stand before Caesar. And God has granted you the lives of all who are sailing with you.’
So take heart, sirs; for I have faith in God that it shall be even as I have been told.
But we must run aground on a certain island.”
On the fourteenth night, as we were drifting across the Adriatic Sea,{k} around midnight the sailors sensed that land was near.
And taking soundings they found a hundred and twenty feet; a little farther on they sounded again and found ninety feet.{l}
And fearing lest we should be cast upon rocky places, they let go four anchors from the stern and longed for day to come.
And as the sailors were seeking to flee from the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea under color of laying out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men abide in the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let her fall off.
While day was coming on, Paul besought them all to partake of food, saying, “This is the fourteenth day you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing.
Therefore I urge you to take some food, for it is for your preservation; for not a hair shall perish from the head of any of you.”
And having said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and broke it and began to eat.
Then they were all encouraged and themselves also took food.
(We were in all about seventy-six persons{m} in the ship.)
And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, casting out the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not recognize the coast, but they saw a bay with a sandy beach, and they decided to try to run the ship aground there.
So casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time loosing the lashings of the steering oars; and hoisting the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.
But striking a place where two seas met,{n} they beached the vessel; the prow stuck and stayed fast, unmoved, while the stern began to go to pieces under the violence of the surf.
The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim off and escape.
But the centurion, wishing to bring Paul safely through, kept them from their purpose, and ordered that those who could swim should cast themselves overboard first and get to land,
and the rest, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass that all were brought safe to land.

notes.text: Julius: a Roman family name, perhaps from Iulus, legendary son of Aeneas; the meaning is uncertain.
Augustan Cohort: or “Imperial Cohort.”
Adramyttium: a port in Mysia, on the northwest coast of Asia Minor.
Myra in Lycia: some Western witnesses add that the crossing took fifteen days.
The Fast: the Day of Atonement, on the tenth of Tishri, in late September or early October, after which sailing on the Mediterranean was considered dangerous.
Southwest and northwest: literally “toward Lips and toward Chorus,” the names of the southwest and northwest winds; the exact sense is uncertain.
Euraquilo: a hybrid of Greek *euros*, “east wind,” and Latin *aquilo*, “north wind”: a northeaster. Many later manuscripts read *Euroclydōn*.
Cauda: many manuscripts read “Clauda.” The island is modern Gavdos, south of Crete.
Syrtis: the gulf of shoals and quicksands off the coast of Libya.
Lowered the gear: perhaps “let down the sea anchor” or “lowered the mainsail”; the Greek is uncertain.
Adriatic Sea: in ancient usage the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy, and Africa, not only the modern Adriatic.
A hundred and twenty feet … ninety feet: literally “twenty fathoms … fifteen fathoms”; about 37 and 27 meters.

Seventy-six persons: so Codex Vaticanus, followed by the Westcott–Hort text. Most manuscripts read “two hundred seventy-six,” and some “two hundred seventy-five.” In Greek numerals the difference may arise from a single letter.
A place where two seas met: or “a sandbar,” “a reef.”

verses.text: Once safe ashore, we learned then that the island was called Malta.{a}
The islanders{b} showed us unusual kindness. Because it had begun to rain and was cold, they built a fire and welcomed all of us.
But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out by reason of the heat and fastened on his hand.
When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said one to another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped the sea, Justice{c} has not suffered to live.”
But he flung the beast off into the flames and took no hurt.
But they were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead; and after they had waited a long while and saw nothing amiss come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius,{d} who received us and entertained us courteously three days.
And it fell out that the father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery; to whom Paul went in, and having prayed and laid his hands on him, he healed him.
When this had taken place, the rest [also] on the island who had diseases came and were cured.
They also honored us with many honors, and when we were setting sail they put on board such things as we needed.
After three months we sailed in a ship from Alexandria that had spent the winter at the island. It carried the Twin Brothers{e} as its figurehead.
Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
And thence we made a circuit{f} and arrived at Rhegium; and after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.
There we found brothers and were entreated to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers there, having had word of us, came out from the city to meet us at Appius’ Market and the Three Inns;{g} and at the sight of them Paul gave God thanks and was heartened.
On our entry into Rome,{h} leave was granted Paul to lodge on his own, along with the soldier set to guard him.

It came to pass after three days that he called together the leading men of the Jews; and when they had come together, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
who, when they had examined me, were minded to release me, because there was no cause for death in me.
But when the Jews objected, I had no choice but to appeal to Caesar, even though I had nothing to accuse my own nation of.
On this account, then, I invited you here, to see you face to face and talk with you; for it is for Israel’s hope that I wear this chain.”
They told him, “For our part, no letters about you have reached us out of Judea, nor has any brother arrived to report or tell anything evil about you.
But we think it fitting to hear from you what your views are; for as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.”

And when they had appointed him a day, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. To them he expounded the matter from morning till evening, testifying to the kingdom of God and seeking to persuade them concerning Jesus from both the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
And some were persuaded by what was spoken, while others disbelieved.
And being at variance among themselves, they departed, after Paul had spoken one word: “Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,

saying,
‘Go to this people, and say,
By hearing you will hear, and shall in no wise understand;
and seeing you will see, and shall in no wise perceive.

For the heart of this people has grown gross,
and with their ears they have heard heavily,
and their eyes they have closed;
lest at any time they should see with their eyes,
and hear with their ears,
and understand with their heart,
and turn again, and I should heal them.’{i}

notes.text: Malta: Greek *Melitē*; the Westcott–Hort text, following Codex Vaticanus, reads *Melitēnē*. The name is perhaps from Phoenician, “refuge,” but the meaning is uncertain.
Natives: Greek *barbaroi*, people who did not speak Greek; the Maltese spoke a Punic dialect.
Justice: Greek *Dikē*, the goddess of justice and retribution.
Publius: a Latin first name, perhaps related to *populus*, “people”; the meaning is uncertain. His title, “chief man” (Greek *prōtos*), is attested on Maltese inscriptions.
The Twin Brothers: Greek *Dioskouroi*, Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus and patrons of sailors.
Made a circuit: some manuscripts read “cast off.”
Appius’ Market and the Three Inns: Latin Forum Appii and Tres Tabernae, stations on the Appian Way, about 43 and 33 miles (69 and 53 km) south of Rome.

Entry into Rome: many manuscripts, mainly Western and Byzantine, add “the centurion delivered the prisoners to the commander of the camp,” and continue “but Paul was allowed to live by himself outside the camp.”
Isa 6:9–10, following the Greek translation of the Old Testament.

The Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts do not include verse 29; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Some later manuscripts add a sentence saying that after Paul spoke, the Jews left, arguing vigorously among themselves.
Hired dwelling: or “at his own expense.”
